summary: Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol (TAP) helps online merchants tell AI shopping agents that Visa has approved apart from other bots. As agents begin to browse shops and pay on behalf of consumers, merchants need a way to let approved agents through while still blocking other automated traffic. TAP is a vendor specification published by Visa in October 2025, developed with Cloudflare, and available on the Visa Developer Center and GitHub under Visa's terms of use.

An approved agent provider signs each request to a merchant with HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421), the same building block as Web Bot Auth, and marks it as browsing or paying. The merchant, or a CDN in front of it, checks the signature against public keys that Visa publishes, a validity window of at most 8 minutes, and a one-time nonce. A request may also carry signed objects describing the consumer (an ID token with a stable identifier and obfuscated contact details) and the payment. TAP does not identify the individual agent, and leaves spending limits, purchase approval (handled by Visa Intelligent Commerce) and revocation outside the protocol.
how_it_works: An agent provider is onboarded with Visa, and its public keys are published in Visa's key store at a well-known location.

When the agent contacts a merchant, it signs the request with an HTTP Message Signature that includes created and expires times, a keyid, a nonce and a tag: agent-browser-auth for browsing or agent-payer-auth for paying.

The request may also carry an Agentic Consumer Recognition Object (information about the consumer) and payment information in an Agentic Payment Container, each signed with the same key and linked by the same nonce.

The merchant, or a site protection provider in front of it (e.g. a CDN), retrieves Visa's public key and checks the signature, the time window of at most 8 minutes and that the nonce has not been seen before. If any check does not pass, the message should be blocked.

If the checks pass, the merchant treats the request as coming from an approved agent and can use the consumer information to recognise its customer. Payment approval and limits are handled by Visa outside TAP.

rows.answer: Visa's protocol where approved shopping agents sign their requests to merchants and attach signed consumer and payment data, so merchants can trust them for browsing and checkout.

rows.answer: Online commerce. A shopping agent interacts with a merchant's website or API at two kinds of moment: browsing and paying. The protocol uses a signature in the HTTP headers plus signed objects in the request body. Verification can be done by the merchant or by a site protection provider in front of it, such as a CDN.

rows.short: Eight participants defined by the spec
rows.answer: Agent Providers: AI platforms onboarded to a payment scheme. Checkout Enablers: services an agent may use to reach merchant sites. Consumers: cardholders with a profile at the agent. Site Protection Providers: a layer in front of the merchant (e.g. CDNs). Identity Provider: verified the consumer's credentials. Merchants: the shops. Payment Schemes: e.g. Visa. Key Store: where public keys are published.

rows.answer: Vendor specification, launched by Visa on 14 October 2025 and developed with Cloudflare, which verifies agent signatures for merchants. Visa also names early partners such as Adyen, Ant International and Checkout.com. It is published on the Visa Developer Center and GitHub under Visa's terms of use, and the specification page shows no version number.

rows.answer: An HTTP Message Signature (RFC 9421) on every request, made with the agent provider's private key. It must include a minimum set of parameters: created and expires times, the keyid, a nonce, and a tag saying whether the agent is browsing (agent-browser-auth) or paying (agent-payer-auth). The consumer and payment objects in the body carry their own signatures with the same key, linked by the same nonce.

rows.answer: Very short. A signature's created and expires times should be no more than 8 minutes apart and must fall around the current time, and merchants should block messages with a longer window. A nonce that has already been seen is also blocked, so each signature can only be used once. Keys themselves can expire, and messages signed with an expired key should be blocked.

rows.answer: Not defined. Visa runs the key store, so it can cut off an agent provider by removing its key; merchants should block messages whose key cannot be retrieved, although a cached key may keep working until each merchant refreshes it. Payments still pass through Visa's network, where they can be stopped. Access can only be cut off for a whole provider, not one agent.

goals_reading.access_control: The merchant learns that the agent comes from a provider Visa has onboarded, and whether it is browsing or paying. Spending limits are enforced by Visa outside the protocol.
goals_reading.incident_response: Visa can cut off a whole agent provider by removing its key, which reaches merchants as their caches refresh, and payments can be stopped in Visa's network. One specific agent cannot be cut off.
goals_reading.accountability: An action can be traced to the agent provider, and to the consumer only when the consumer recognition object is sent.

notes: Calibration example for the protocol-analyzer skill (Visa TAP specification page as accessed on 2026-11-18).
The specification page uses lowercase requirement words (should, may) rather than RFC 2119 keywords. Requirement tags with an asterisk reflect this.
The Visa sites block scripted downloads, so their quotes were checked with a web tool (WEB-OK). The web tool limits quotes to about 125 characters, so some quotes are sentence fragments.
The specification page shows no version number or date, so it may change without notice.
open_questions: Which merchants verify TAP signatures in production, beyond Cloudflare as a verifier?
